input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

new paragraph before we close up i want to check the accession cards for the shells and match them to the old ledger especially the card for the spiral shell with the chipped lip the ledger lists a parcel from north field but there is no collection date beside it and the card says acquired from mr hall in 1964 i cannot tell whether that is the same shell or a different one so leave both entries as they are for now if you have time tomorrow please read the two descriptions with me and we can compare the handwriting the collection is mostly in good order but i am leaving this memo because several small details are easy to lose when the drawers are open", "output": "Hi Mara, this is my voice memo about the fossil collection before I go back to the east room tomorrow. I want to record what I moved and what still needs attention, because I keep mixing up the cabinets in my notes. The collection is in the old map room now, not the basement. The basement shelves are still being checked for damp, and I have not taken anything down there yet. The room has one narrow window facing the courtyard, and the afternoon light reaches the worktable but not the cabinets, which is useful for keeping the labels readable.

The main cabinet is oak, and it has six shallow drawers. The top drawer is for small fish and plant impressions. The second drawer has shell fossils from the gray limestone block that came from the farm above Bell Creek. The third drawer holds trilobites and a few pieces that might be crinoid stems, but I am not sure about those yet. The fourth drawer is empty except for a folded map and a paper packet marked quarry edge. The fifth drawer has the larger ammonites, and the bottom one has plaster casts that should not be stored beside the originals. I started to move them yesterday and then remembered the casts are heavier than they look, so I left them where they were.

Section 1: Items that need a new label: tray seven; the small slab with two fern marks; the broken shell with the blue thread tied around it; the three little fish scales in the envelope from June; and the sandstone piece that has no number at all. I thought the fern slab was from the ridge site, but the notebook says lower pit, so use lower pit unless someone finds a later note. The blue thread is not part of the fossil; it was put there by my uncle to match the shell to his sketch, and the thread has started to fray.

Yesterday Professor Ellis came by for about twenty minutes and said, “The ridge layers may be older than we first thought.” She did not give a date, and she was talking about the field notes, not a finished analysis. She looked at the ammonites and asked whether the label was written by my grandfather. I said I think so, because the capital R is the same as in his letters, but I have not checked the writing against the family box yet. She also asked me not to clean the brown film off the spiral one until she can look at it under the lens. I have put a card on that drawer, but the card only says leave for Ellis.

There are two notebooks in the green case. The small one has observations from 1978 through 1981, and the larger one starts in 1982. The larger notebook has a loose page between April and May with a drawing of a tooth and the words west cut written at the top. I do not know if west cut means the excavation area or the western face of the cut, so do not add a more specific place to the catalog description. The page has three pencil circles along the edge and a coffee stain over one line. I can still read the phrase “pale band below the dark seam,” but the rest looks rubbed away.

For the packing table, I have put clean tissue on the left side and the padded trays on the right. There are four trays in the stack, not three. The top one is for the tiny pieces, the second is for the two large shells, the third is for the stone fragments, and the bottom tray is empty. I put the empty tray there because the lid is cracked on one corner, and it should not be stacked on the fossils. There is also a brass ruler by the lamp and a little brush in a jar. Please keep the brush with the table, because it belongs to the collection kit, not the office supplies.

The drawer keys are on a ring inside the blue cup by the sink. I counted five keys, but only four have tags. The small brass key opens the cabinet, and the long flat key opens the map case. I do not know what the short silver key fits, and the fourth tagged key has a paper label that says back room, even though it does not turn the basement lock. I have not tried the untagged key in any of the doors, because I do not want to force it. If you find a key chart in the desk drawer, can you take a photograph before moving it?

There is a damp mark under the courtyard window, but it is dry to the touch today, and the paper label on the fossil crate is still flat. I put a folded towel under the crate yesterday as a precaution. The towel is dry too. The radiator made a clicking sound twice around four o’clock and then stopped. I do not know whether that has anything to do with the mark, but I wrote down the time in case it happens again. There is a faint smell like wet stone near the lower cabinet and no smell near the table. I have not found any water on the floor.

Before we close up, I want to check the accession cards for the shells and match them to the old ledger, especially the card for the spiral shell with the chipped lip. The ledger lists a parcel from north field, but there is no collection date beside it, and the card says acquired from Mr Hall in 1964. I cannot tell whether that is the same shell or a different one, so leave both entries as they are for now. If you have time tomorrow, please read the two descriptions with me, and we can compare the handwriting. The collection is mostly in good order, but I am leaving this memo because several small details are easy to lose when the drawers are open."}, {"id": "arka-v3b-train-transcribe-0065", "row_sha256": "ce4cd640d267e6f495659e91b803a33279a2515eff76b64a6dd2687f3602872d", "mode": "/transcribe", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Remove true hesitation and accidental restarts. Keep the supplied language.", "input": "monday at seven ten i unlocked the pump room and checked the log before starting anything the filter pressure was eighteen psi which is two higher than friday so i wrote that down first the west skimmer had two leaves no three leaves packed against the basket i cleared them and rinsed the basket at the hose tap the water level was just below the middle of the tile line so i topped it up for about twelve minutes then checked the pump lid for a seal leak there was a little water on the outside but it was old splash not a drip i ran the circulation pump and listened for air in the line it sounded steady after a minute i tested the pool water chlorine was one point five and ph was seven point six i added no chemicals because both readings were in the range on the sheet i brushed the shallow end steps and the ledge by the ladder then vacuumed the fine grit along the drain i put the vacuum hose back on its rack and left the pump running the next check is after lunch if the pressure is still above twenty i should rinse the filter and note the new reading in the log", "output": "Monday at seven ten, I unlocked the pump room and checked the log before starting anything. The filter pressure was eighteen psi, which is two higher than Friday, so I wrote that down first. The west skimmer had three leaves packed against the basket. I cleared them and rinsed the basket at the hose tap. The water level was just below the middle of the tile line, so I topped it up for about twelve minutes, then checked the pump lid for a seal leak. There was a little water on the outside, but it was old splash, not a drip. I ran the circulation pump and listened for air in the line. It sounded steady after a minute. I tested the pool water: chlorine was one point five, and pH was seven point six. I added no chemicals because both readings were in the range on the sheet. I brushed the shallow-end steps and the ledge by the ladder, then vacuumed the fine grit along the drain. I put the vacuum hose back on its rack and left the pump running.
